main_issue: The two evidenced cases share a broad authorization-bypass outcome but use different mechanisms: one selects an incorrect authorization policy during group/object resolution, while the other exposes a privileged tenant-management handler without an endpoint permission gate. The current resource-ID/ownership-scope query does not accurately target the policy-selection defect and overstates unsupported IDOR-like shapes.
suggested_guideline: Split this group into (1) authorization-policy selection/precedence errors, where code resolves a protected parent object or privilege from a collection of policies without matching the policy to the intended group, principal, action, or default-policy semantics; require an explicit semantic match before returning or applying the protected object; and (2) missing authorization gates on sensitive controller or RPC handlers, where tenant, membership, invitation, workflow, or administrative actions are reachable without the required permission annotation or equivalent centralized authorization check; require the guard on the request-to-effect path.
split_suggestions: Authorization-policy resolution selects the wrong policy or protected object because matching/precedence semantics are incomplete
Sensitive endpoint performs tenant or administrative action without a required method-level or centralized permission guard
evidence_notes: DSpace CVE-2021-41189 evidence indicates getParentObject returns the first candidate policy instead of selecting the policy matching the intended default read group; this is policy-resolution/authorization-logic confusion rather than a user-controlled resource-ID ownership check.
JEECG CVE-2025-14908 evidence indicates tenant membership/invitation handlers lack a method-level permission gate or are removed by the patch; this is a missing endpoint authorization guard.
The supplied evidence does not establish unauthenticated access, generic IDOR, deletion paths, or a common checked-identity-to-data-access propagation defect across both cases.
